33.0.big: The immune system defends the body (the host) against pathogens with two layers: a fast, general innate defense and a slower, targeted adaptive defense with memory.
points: Immune cells are white blood cells. Many travel through lymph, the fluid of the lymphatic system.

33.1.big: Innate immunity is the defense you're born with: barriers plus cells and proteins that attack any invader quickly.
points: Barriers: dry, acidic skin; mucus; tears and saliva with enzymes; stomach acid; helpful bacteria.
Recognition: pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) on immune cells detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), parts common to many germs. That triggers cytokine signals.
Phagocytes eat invaders: macrophages (develop from monocytes), neutrophils, and dendritic cells. Engulfed microbes are destroyed by lysosomes.
Inflammation: mast cells (and basophils) release histamine → vessels widen and leak → redness, heat, swelling, and more immune cells arrive. Eosinophils fight parasites.
Infected cells release interferons, which warn nearby cells to resist viruses.
Natural killer (NK) cells check for MHC I "self" markers on body cells. Cells missing it (infected or cancerous) are killed with perforin (punches holes) and granzymes (trigger cell death).
The complement system: about 20 blood proteins that activate each other in a cascade to coat germs (opsonization, which speeds up phagocytosis) and punch holes in them.

33.2.big: Adaptive immunity learns: it builds a specific attack against each new antigen and remembers it, so the next response is faster and stronger.
points: Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells) eat germs and display pieces on MHC II molecules. Every body cell shows its own proteins on MHC I.
Lymphocytes: B cells mature in bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus. Each recognizes one specific antigen.
Helper T lymphocytes (TH) bind antigen on an APC's MHC II, then release cytokines that activate B cells and killer T cells. HIV destroys these CD4⁺ cells.
Cell-mediated immune response: cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) kill infected cells that show foreign antigen on MHC I.
Humoral immune response: activated B cells become plasma cells that pump out antibodies.
Clonal selection: the one lymphocyte that matches an antigen multiplies into many effector cells plus long-lived memory cells. That's why vaccines work.
Regulatory T (Treg) cells calm the response and help keep immune tolerance (not attacking self). Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) guards the gut and airways.
Passive immunity = borrowed antibodies (from mother through the placenta or milk, or an antibody shot). Short-lived, with no memory.
33.2.tip: B cells make antiBodies. T cells Take out infected cells (or help everyone else).

33.3.big: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein whose tips fit one specific part of an antigen like a lock and key.
points: Structure: two heavy chains + two light chains. The variable regions at the tips bind the antigen. The constant region decides the antibody's class (IgM first, IgG most common, IgA in mucus and milk, IgE in allergies, IgD).
The exact spot an antibody binds is the epitope.
Diversity: in each B cell, DNA segments are randomly cut and rejoined (by DNA recombinase) before transcription, making over a trillion different antibodies from a few genes.
Affinity = how tightly one binding site holds. Avidity = total binding strength with all sites. Cross reactivity = an antibody also binding a similar, different antigen.
Jobs: neutralize toxins and viruses, coat germs for phagocytes (opsonization), clump them together, and activate complement.

33.4.big: Problems arise when immunity is too weak, overreacts to harmless things, or attacks the body itself.
points: Immunodeficiency: a weak or missing immune response, either inherited (SCID) or acquired (HIV/AIDS destroys helper T cells).
Hypersensitivities come in three types: immediate (allergies), delayed (like a poison ivy rash), and autoimmune.
Allergy: an immune response to something harmless (pollen, peanuts). IgE on mast cells triggers histamine release. Antihistamines block histamine's effects.

Autoimmunity (an autoimmune response): the body attacks itself with autoantibodies. Examples: type 1 diabetes (insulin-making cells), Graves' disease (antibodies switch on the thyroid), myasthenia gravis (antibodies block acetylcholine receptors on muscle).

1.why: Skin is dry (and acidic), so most microbes can't survive on it.

2.why: These bacteria only grow between pH 5.4 and 7.4. Skin that keeps them out would be outside that range (skin is actually about pH 5).

3.why: Macrophages recognize and engulf invaders right away.

4.why: Damaged cells and immune cells release cytokines and histamine, which cause inflammation.

5.why: NK cells check for MHC I and kill cells without it.

6.why: NK cells kill by lysis (perforin, granzymes). Macrophages eat invaders.

8.why: MHC I displays protein pieces on the cell surface.

9.why: About 20 blood proteins that attack in a cascade.

10.why: Complement coats germs, so phagocytes engulf them faster.

12.why: You build a specific response after exposure, and it's remembered for next time.

13.why: Mast cells are innate. T cells, B cells and antibodies are adaptive.

16.why: At step 2 the B cell is displaying pieces of the antigen on its surface, ready for helper T cells.

17.why: Binding a different but similar antigen = cross reactivity.

18.why: One antibody binding several proteins = cross reactivity.

20.why: Different constant regions = different antibody classes (IgG, IgM, IgA...).

21.why: DNA recombinase cuts and rejoins the gene segments.

22.why: DNA rearranges first, then transcription → RNA processing → translation.

23.why: What's measured, lung function, is the dependent variable.

24.why: It reacts to something harmless that needs no defense.

26.why: Autoantibodies attack the body's own insulin-making cells, causing inflammation and damage.

29.why: Some entry points (mouth, nose, eyes) aren't covered by skin.

30.why: NK cells act immediately on cells missing self markers. Interferons are induced after infection is detected.

31.why: The recipient's NK cells see the donor's MHC I as non-self and attack.

32.why: Without MHC I, the immune system can't tell self from non-self (or spot infected cells).

33.why: Yes: it's a cascade, so a broken early step stops everything after it.

34.why: Pathogens keep changing. One adaptable system that can make specific responses to new germs saves energy and storage.

35.why: Everyone has innate immunity, so it came first. Adaptive appeared after vertebrates split off, early in vertebrate history.

36.why: Naïve = not yet exposed. Once activated, B cells make antibodies and T cells do cell-mediated attacks.

37.why: The vaccine made antibodies to one strain. January's virus was different enough that those antibodies didn't protect.

38.why: Variable regions let the body make antibodies with many different targets.

39.why: Mother's antibodies cross the placenta: passive immunity.

40.why: Allergies react to harmless environmental proteins. Teaching the body to treat them as "self" would stop that.

41.why: Their immune system makes antibodies against their own salivary gland proteins.

42.why: A dip right away, recovery, then a bigger dip hours later (the late phase).

43.why: Phagocytes destroy engulfed bacteria by fusing them with lysosomes.

44.why: NK cells see MHC I on healthy cells and spare them. Infected cells that lose MHC I are killed.

45.why: Pathogen (has PAMPs) → dendritic cell (has PRRs, releases cytokines) → protects healthy host cells.

46.why: Helper T cells are a required step in activating B cells. No helpers = no antibodies.

47.why: The macrophage shows antigen on an MHC molecule, and the T cell receptor binds it.

48.why: APCs display vaccine antigen, helper T cells bind it, and that contact leads to B cells making antibodies.

49.why: Helper T cells release cytokines that help B cells multiply into plasma cells.

50.why: Antibodies grab the toxins, so they can't bind receptors and enter cells (neutralization).

51.why: In the B cell, the V and C pieces are on the same fragment: the DNA was rearranged.

52.why: Each antibody has a specific antigen-binding site that fits only its target.

53.why: Specific antibodies = effective. Not needing a gene per antibody = efficient.

54.why: Antihistamines block histamine from acting on tissues, so less itching and swelling.

55.why: Autoantibodies keep the TSH receptor switched on no matter what, so negative feedback fails and too much thyroid hormone is made.

56.why: Antibodies block the acetylcholine receptors on muscle, so signals don't get through.
